title: Feminist and Gender Studies in Theatre and Performance
description: Advanced problems in feminist theories of theatre and performance. In addition to gender theory, examination of feminist perspectives on dramatichistory and criticism.

title: Reading Intercultural Drama
description: Examination of intercultural theory, practice, and dramatic literature. Material may include playwrights ranging from Shakespeare to David Henry Hwang, and practitioners and theorists such as Augusto Boal, Eugenio Barba, and Anne Bogart.

title: Modern British Drama: Osborne to Present
description: Study of major contemporary playwrights.

title: Topics in Dramatic Literature and Theatre History
description: A survey course that introduces students to a range of historical periods, dramatic work, playwrights, artistic movements, and theatrical trends. Topics vary and may include classics in performance, translating drama, global theatre, violence in drama, dramatic genre, and literature and theatre.

title: Adaptation
description: Adaptation and translation for the stage: Including work from other genres like prose, film, opera, song, poetry, myth, or plays written in a previous era. Also works from other languages, especially Spanish). The original source should be text-based. Students read variations of ANTIGONE, MEDEA, DON JUAN and other adaptations. The final project consists of a play or performance piece at least forty pages in length, not necessarily the finished product, but perhaps the beginning of a much larger work

title: African Theatre and Drama
description: Examines key concepts in 20th century and contemporary African theatre: the reconstruction of identity formations in the wake of decolonization, intersections of indigenous and re-created performance modes, cultural flows of people and dramatic texts across national borders, myths and oral traditions, and representations of gender, race, and ethnicity. Drawing on a wide spectrum of plays and critical texts, we interrogate how theatre functions in the often - tumultuous political and social milieus of African nations.

title: Asian Theatre and Drama
description: Dramatic literature and staged theater of Asia. Coverage varies from traditional to contemporary dramatists and theatre styles from East Asia to India and/or Southeast Asia. Reception of Asian theatre in non-Asian contexts is often considered.

title: Shakespeare Beyond the Global
description: Shakespeare has reigned as a global phenomenon in text, performance and film for over thirty years. But why? What is a global Shakespeare? How was a global Shakespeare devised? Can we move beyond the global? Can we think beyond the global? By considering these lines of inquiry, this seminar seeks to investigate the formations of Shakespeare as a global icon, global commodity, and global performance framework. We will also think through the violent histories of colonialism, racialization and empire that undergird the "Global Shakespeare '' movement. Authors and practitioners include: Preti Taneja, Kim F. Hall, Alexa Joubin, Ambereen Dadabhoy, Vishal Bharadwaj, Akira Kurosawa, Madeline Sayet, Sujata Iyengar, Ruben Espinosa, Gauri Viswanathan.

title: Don Juan through the Ages
description: Explores dramatic manifestations of the Don Juan theme (including history and criticism) from Tirso de Molina (17th century), Moliere, Mozarts Don Giovanni, Jose Zorrillas Romantic version, and into the 20th century with Shaw and Brecht. Also Don Juan in the New World via Derek Walcott, Mortons Johnny Tenorio, Octavio Solis, and Anne Garcia-Romero. Students write papers and present oral reports comparing and contrasting different versions and/or adaptations of the Don Juan theme in dramatic literature

title: Playwriting and Dramaturgy
description: An investigation of the art of playwriting in terms of the dramaturgy of how plays work.

title: Race, Pedagogy, and Theatre
description: Examines critical intersections between racial identities and performance practices, such as casting, season selection, acting, directing, comedy, and dance. To understand how race functions as a historical and cultural construct, we will read foundational plays and other texts to consider how diverse writers and artists cultivate and constitute new understandings of race through imaginative performances. We will also explore how notions of race become contested and championed through casting and production practices at mainstream and ethnically-specific venues.

title: Topics in Dramatic Literature, Theatre History, and Performance Practices
description: This course investigates the intersections between art, literature, philosophy, and performance practices. It may include specific histories of theatre and performance, conceptual frames across cultures, genre studies, issues of translation, postcolonial analysis, and other topics.

title: The Fate of Ophelia: Shakespeare and Popular Culture
description: This graduate seminar examines how Shakespeare circulates through contemporary popular culture. Though rooted in the early modern stage, Shakespeare's characters, plots, and language now form a global cultural vocabulary, appearing across film, television, music, fashion, advertising, and digital media. The course treats Shakespeare not as fixed canon but as a dynamic cultural resource that artists and audiences continually transform to speak to new historical moments. Drawing on adaptation studies, performance theory, and cultural criticism, the seminar explores why Shakespeare remains so culturally influential and how his works move across media and genres

title: Sexuality and Race in Early/Modernity
description: Explores histories of sex, sexuality, and race in performance. With a focus on historical contexts of empire, global economies of trade, travels and discoveries, conversions, and slavery, the course aims to recognize genealogies of contemporary intersections of sexuality/race, revealing continuities, ruptures, and crossings between discourses and practices as they emerge in performance in the past and present. Pushing temporal and disciplinary boundaries, the seminar investigates directions and inquiries in early modern sexuality studies, race studies, queer theory, and performance studies.

title: Special Topics in Performance Studies
description: Varies in content from year to year, but offerings may include studies of the avant-garde and performance art, sport as ritual and performance, theatre on trial, politics and war as performance, embodiment, and global performance traditions.

title: African Performance Studies
description: Examines the broad field of performance in Africa and the African diaspora, including ritual, storytelling, oral traditions, masquerades, festivals, dance, truth commissions, and spirit possession.

title: Border Crossings: Exilic Experience in the Making of American Dance
description: Border Crossing challenges accepted histories of dance modernism to consider how war, inequality, and injustice shaped twentieth century performance art. This graduate seminar bears witness to the exiled and marginalized dance artist - the Unsung - whose artistry, oftentimes invisible, is vital to the history of dance.

title: Masculinities in/as Performance
description: Explores the intersection of masculinity IN performance (theater, dance, performance art, film/TV, internet platforms, etc.), and AS performance. Topics include maleness/masculinity as a social construct, considerations of masculinity in adolescent development and pedagogy, implications of race and class: marginalized masculinities, female masculinity, trans-masculinity, etc. These lenses are then employed to consider how masculinity forms identity and frames representation within various performative platforms.

title: Special Topics in Performance Studies
description: Exploration of the history and theory of story and storytelling, both in its relation to dramatic and/or choreographed plot and as a performance mode in itself.

title: Critical Dance Studies: Special Topics in Dance History and Theory
description: This graduate seminar provides an introduction to the history and critical theory of dance inglobal contexts. The methodologicalfocus may include critical dance studies, historiography,ethnography, feminist theory, critical race theory, body theory - corporealities - art and architectural(site-specific performance) theory, and performance studies. Students read and analyze a widearray of critics, scholars, and artists and demonstrate fluency in critical dance studies through writtenpapers and weekly seminar discussion. Live Performance serves as archival source material.

title: Defiant Bodies: Art, Dance, Digital Media
description: Defiant Bodies: Art, Dance, Digital Media surveys an interdisciplinary array of visual art, digital media, and live performance. Together, we identify historiographic relationships between protest culture, human philosophy, and performance.

title: Border Crossings: Exilic Experience in the Making of Modern Dance
description: Border Crossings: Exilic Experience in the Making of American Dance, challenges previous histories of transglobal modernism to consider how war, inequality, and injustice shaped twentieth century performance art. The intellectual, pedagogical, and spiritual embodiment of a bicoastal exhibit and performance series, together as an intellectual community of scholar-artists, we investigate definitions of exile and exilic modernism as each engenders methodologies in the fields of Dance Studies and Performance Studies.
